turns.content: My best friend Shreya's wedding festivities got dated — and her sangeet plus cocktail night is smack in the middle of Ramzan. I'll be fasting. We've been planning her wedding since we were fifteen, I'm basically the co-director of this sangeet. She keeps saying "you HAVE to do the opening dance with me." I want to. And I'm dreading all of it.

Oh, that sounds so tough. You're caught between two really important things - your commitment to your best friend who's been planning this wedding with you for over a decade, and your religious practice during Ramzan. 

It makes total sense that you're dreading this. When you've been someone's wedding "co-director" since you were fifteen, and she's counting on that opening dance, that's not just a casual commitment. That's years of friendship and shared dreams right there.

And honestly, the fact that you're even worrying about this shows how much you care about both Shreya and your faith. Sometimes life puts us in these impossible positions where doing right by one person feels like it means letting down another. 

Have you and Shreya talked about how you'll handle the dancing and the festivities while you're fasting? I imagine she wants you there more than anything, even if it means adjusting plans a bit.

Yesterday she said, with total love, "one day of fasting won't matter na, I'll feed you myself." She wasn't being mean — she just doesn't know what she's asking. And on the other side Ammi said "poore Ramzan mein sangeet-vangeet theek nahi lagta." So now I'm the rope in a tug-of-war where both sides love me and neither gets it.

Ugh, that's the worst feeling - being the rope in a tug-of-war where everyone's pulling with love. Shreya saying "one day won't matter" comes from a place of genuine affection, but it's like someone saying "just one sip of water won't break your diet" - they don't understand it's not about the physical act itself, it's about the commitment and meaning behind it.

And Ammi's "sangeet-vangeet theek nahi lagta" is her way of protecting you and your spiritual well-being, even if it feels restrictive right now.

You're right in the middle of two completely valid perspectives that just don't speak the same language. Shreya speaks friendship-language, Ammi speaks faith-language, and you're trying to translate between them while your own heart is getting squeezed.

The beautiful, frustrating thing is that both of them are right from their own viewpoints. Shreya is right that she needs you there, and Ammi is right that Ramzan has a certain sacred rhythm that shouldn't be disrupted.

Have you thought about what your own heart needs in this? Like, what would make you feel like you're honoring both your friendship and your faith in a way that feels authentic to you?

Honestly I'm so tired that I've started drafting the escape: I tell Shreya there's an office deployment that week, do a video call appearance, send a big gift. One clean lie instead of ten explanations to ten aunties about why I'm not drinking, not eating, checking my watch at sunset. She'd never know. Tell me that's not terrible?

Oh, I get why that feels tempting. The idea of one clean lie that solves everything - no awkward explanations, no watching everyone else enjoy food and drink while you're counting down the minutes, no feeling like you have to choose between your friend and your faith.

But here's the thing - Shreya isn't just any friend. You've been planning this wedding since you were fifteen. You're the co-director. This isn't some casual acquaintance you can ghost with a plausible excuse.

And think about it this way - if you lie, you're not just avoiding one difficult day. You're potentially losing something much bigger: that moment when she realizes her best friend wasn't there for one of the most important celebrations of her life. The "office deployment" excuse might work for aunties, but Shreya? She knows you better than that.

The exhaustion you're feeling is real, but lying to your best friend about her wedding might leave you feeling even more empty than fasting through a sangeet.

What if there was a middle path? Like being there but finding ways to honor your fast that don't feel like you're hiding? Or having an honest conversation with Shreya about how much this means to you?

And under all of it there's this small stone in my chest — this is the first time in eighteen years of friendship that my deen and her big day have actually collided. If I get this wrong, one of two things I love gets a permanent dent. Her shaadi photos will exist forever, and so will my Ramzan. I don't want to be a sad story in either album.

That stone in your chest... it's heavy because it's holding the weight of eighteen years of friendship and eighteen years of faith, right there in one moment. And you're absolutely right - those photos will exist forever, and so will your Ramzan.

But here's what I see that maybe you're not seeing: this collision isn't necessarily going to create a dent in either story. Sometimes the most beautiful stories are the ones where love shows up in its most complicated form.

Think about it - Shreya's wedding album will have one photo where she's dancing with her best friend, who chose to honor her faith even when it meant missing some of the festivities. That's not a sad story. That's a story of integrity, of love that's big enough to hold both friendship and faith.

And your Ramzan? This year's Ramadan will have a story about how you navigated a difficult moment with grace, how you showed up for your friend in ways that weren't about food or dancing but about presence and loyalty. That's not a sad story either.

You're not choosing between two things you love. You're learning how to love both things in their fullness, even when they're messy together.

What if this moment becomes the thing that makes both your friendship and your faith deeper, not the thing that dents them?
